title: Crash on insert or deletion into compressed chunk
body: When we try to insert data into a compressed chunk, the database crashes. I reported TimescaleDB 2.14.2 with PostgreSQL 15.6 on Ubuntu 20.04.2 x64, deployed through Docker on AWS. The logs show the database entering recovery, connections being reset, and repeated DELETE statements against the signal hypertable failing while recovery is in progress. I believe this may be related to issue #6031.

symptoms_visible: When I write data involving a compressed chunk, the database crashes, connections are reset, and the server enters recovery mode.
The surrounding logs repeatedly mention DELETE FROM signal while the database is recovering.
N0.label: N0 compressed-chunk crash reported

symptoms_visible: The production database still crashes during an upload that deletes a time range and then writes replacement signal data.
N1.label: N1 schema and write sequence collected

symptoms_visible: Running a simple DELETE by itself against the affected compressed time range terminates the server process with signal 11.
N2_x.label: N2_x COPY diagnosis rejected by isolated DELETE

symptoms_visible: The same standalone DELETE still causes a segmentation fault in the PostgreSQL server process.
N3.label: N3 server-side backtrace collected

symptoms_visible: The production crash has not yet been retested after confirming and updating the loaded TimescaleDB extension version.
N4.label: N4 reported version questioned

symptoms_visible: After using TimescaleDB 2.14.2, the compressed-chunk DELETE no longer crashes; I can reproduce the issue only on 2.14.0.
N_terminal.label: terminal version correction verified

question_patterns: Can you share the hypertable schema definitions and indexes?
What are the definitions of the affected signal and aggregated hypertables?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The signal hypertable has bigint id, timestamp time, and double precision value, with indexes on (id, time DESC) and time DESC. The aggregated hypertable has id, time, duration, integral, rising_edges, min, max, and level. Both use ten-day chunks and currently have roughly 360 child tables.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: These are ordinary PostgreSQL tables and none of the affected rows are in TimescaleDB hypertables or compressed chunks.
The same columns and indexes are present, but the chunk interval is seven days rather than ten days.

question_patterns: What compression policy or commands do you use?
How and when are the affected chunks compressed?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: A Kubernetes cronjob runs once a week. It calls compress_chunk for signal and aggregated chunks whose range_end is more than 91 days old, then runs VACUUM ANALYZE.

question_patterns: What SQL does one upload execute, including the DELETE and COPY?
Can you show the relevant write sequence from the application?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: For each upload I start a serializable transaction, DELETE the existing id and time range, COPY the replacement points with COPY signal (id, time, value) FROM STDIN BINARY, and INSERT the final null point with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: There is no DELETE in the transaction; the crash happens during a standalone COPY into an old compressed chunk.

edges.comment: From c1-c4 and c7, all describing the reporter's own production schema, compression cronjob, and Rust upload transaction.

solution.intent: Treat COPY into a compressed chunk as the crash source and avoid it by using INSERT or decompressing the chunks before COPY.
solution.concrete_example: Replace COPY with INSERT for this upload, or decompress the destination chunks before running COPY.

edges.comment: From c3, c8, and c10: the COPY theory and workaround were proposed, but the reporter then reproduced the segmentation fault with a standalone DELETE in production. The maintainer explicitly concluded that the COPY-related fix would not solve this case.

question_patterns: Can you collect a server-side stack trace with gdb when the DELETE crashes?
Please attach gdb to the PostgreSQL process and share the crash backtrace.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I attached gdb to the PostgreSQL server process and captured the backtrace. The output reaches TimescaleDB's tsl/src/compression/compression.c around line 2553, and I shared the corresponding source link.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The backtrace never enters TimescaleDB code; it crashes entirely inside an unrelated native extension.
The same compression.c frame appears, but with slightly different surrounding PostgreSQL frames.

edges.comment: From c11-c16 on the reporter's system: maintainers requested a gdb stack trace, and the reporter supplied raw debugger output plus the source-line URL. No additional mechanism is inferred from the frame here.

solution.intent: Inspect the expression fields in the coredump to determine why the compression code received an unexpected expression shape.
solution.concrete_example: Inspect opexpr->args and the other opexpr fields in the coredump near the reported compression.c frame before assuming the earlier COPY bug applies.

edges.comment: From c17-c18: a maintainer requested deeper coredump inspection. Before producing it, the reporter volunteered that the loaded extension might actually still have been 2.14.0 because the database update command may not have been run. This was the reporter's own deployment, not another participant's setup.

solution.intent: Verify the extension version actually loaded by PostgreSQL, complete the update from 2.14.0 to 2.14.2 if needed, and retest the standalone DELETE before declaring a TimescaleDB 2.14.2 crash.
solution.concrete_example: Check the TimescaleDB extension version loaded in the database rather than relying on the Docker image tag. If it is still 2.14.0, run the required extension update to 2.14.2 and then execute the same standalone DELETE again.

edges.comment: Resolution from c18-c20 on the reporter's own deployment: after questioning whether the database extension had been updated, the reporter later confirmed that the crash applied only to 2.14.0 and was nonexistent on 2.14.2. No unconfirmed source-level mechanism or later main-branch guard is treated as the accepted root cause.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause as a version mismatch: despite the opening report naming 2.14.2, the affected database was effectively on TimescaleDB 2.14.0 because the extension update may not have been run; the reporter confirmed the crash does not exist on 2.14.2.

Must ground the diagnosis in the collected evidence: an isolated DELETE reproduced signal 11, the gdb backtrace entered the compression code, and the reporter later questioned and verified the actual extension version.

Must not attribute this case to COPY or rely on replacing COPY with INSERT or decompressing before COPY as the fix; a standalone DELETE reproduced the crash and the maintainer explicitly rejected the COPY-related fix for this issue.
Must verify the loaded database extension version rather than relying only on the Docker image or initially reported version.
Must ask the reporter to rerun the same DELETE after updating to 2.14.2 and treat the issue as resolved only after the reporter confirms that it no longer crashes.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced backend operator and developer who can provide PostgreSQL schemas, application SQL and Rust code, reproduce a query with psql, and collect a server-side gdb backtrace, but initially conflated the Docker image version with the extension version loaded in the database.
persona_hint.communication_style: Cooperative and technically detailed; shares exact SQL, logs, code, and debugger output; openly corrects earlier assumptions and asks maintainers to pause when verification is pending.
